39: This plan describes a Neapolitan-style pizza shop built around a wood-fired oven the guests can see, in a mid-sized American city of 150,000 to 300,000 people, on a neighborhood street with foot traffic or next to a plaza. The space is about 1,500 sq ft (139 sq m) with a flue to the roof, a dining room of {{aforo}} seats and a 24-seat patio from April to October, and it is leased as a second-generation space. It is run by a single-owner LLC: you as head pizzaiolo and general manager, a second pizzaiolo, a helper, front of house in two shifts and extra weekend help. It opens in September, Tuesday through Sunday, for lunch and dinner, and closes on Mondays and for two weeks in January. The menu is short and built on long-fermented dough.
40: The key figures of the example case are these. We average {{clientes_dia}} covers a day across the dining room, take-out and delivery, at an average check of {{ticket}} excluding sales tax, over {{dias}} opening days. That produces {{ventas_a1}} in year-1 revenue and a net profit of {{resultado_neto_a1}}, or {{margen_neto_a1}} of sales. The average includes the ramp-up: the Excel spreads the year month by month, and Month 1 is September. Accounting break-even is {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} covers a day, and cash break-even, which also covers the loan payments, is {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}}. That net margin is far below the 15-25% that some online templates promise; PMQ's 2026 Pizza Power Report quotes 2-3% for lean independents, so we would rather show you an honest number. It is not a guaranteed return but a starting point: change the assumptions and enter your own figures.
41: Total startup investment is {{inversion_total}}: {{capex}} for build-out, oven, equipment and opening, which includes the security deposit and {{meses_alquiler_previo}} months of rent paid before opening, plus a {{fondo_maniobra}} working capital reserve. The cash needed at opening comes to {{necesidad_caja}}. It is funded with {{fondos_propios}} of your own money ({{aportacion_pct}} of the total) and a {{prestamo}} SBA 7(a) loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} over {{plazo_prestamo}} years. The annual loan payment is {{cuota_anual}}. Sales tax is collected from guests and passed on to the state, so it never enters the investment.
42: Year 1 brings in {{ventas_a1}} with a net profit of {{resultado_neto_a1}}. Covers grow {{crecimiento_a2}} in year 2 and {{crecimiento_a3}} in year 3 at the same average check, so revenue rises to {{ventas_a2}} and {{ventas_a3}}, and net profit to {{resultado_neto_a2}} and {{resultado_neto_a3}}. The margin of safety over cash break-even is {{holgura_caja_pct}}, and the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) never falls below {{dscr_min}} over the life of the loan, against the {{dscr_objetivo}} that lenders typically look for. Payback before debt comes from the cash flow in the Excel: {{payback}} with the working capital reserve counted in the investment, and {{payback_capex}} on startup costs alone.
43: The team is small and leans on you. You are the head pizzaiolo and run the oven and the dough every day. Alongside you are a second pizzaiolo, a helper, front of house in two shifts and weekend help, for {{plantilla_puestos}} people on the payroll who add up to {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents. The kit includes this ten-section business plan, the nine-sheet financial projections in Excel, the 80-task startup checklist in six phases, the pizza dough and food cost calculator, and the Equivalents Guide.
46: Not every pizza business is the same business, and it pays to choose before you sign anything. The wood-fired sit-down pizza shop, which is the model in this plan, makes its dough daily and sells an experience, but it takes the biggest investment and a space that can take a flue. The New York-style slice shop lives on a small footprint and heavy volume, with a low check. The delivery-only kitchen starts with less build-out but depends on marketplace commissions and an algorithm you do not control. A franchise brings a brand and a method in exchange for royalties and little freedom on the menu. Each model has its own investment, space and margin, and this plan takes the first because it builds a product that is yours.
47: The value proposition is long-fermented dough made fresh every day and a wood-fired oven in plain view, so guests watch it work from their table. The menu is short, 14 to 16 pizzas, with Italian ingredients such as San Marzano tomatoes (DOP) and fior di latte, Neapolitan-inspired starters like frittatina, montanarina or burrata, and three house-made desserts. The dough comes first: you weigh flour, water, salt and yeast in grams and work in baker's percentages, mix gently, bulk ferment, ball the dough and cold ferment it, then stretch each pizza by hand, never with a rolling pin. Wood has a practical side as well as flavor: it gives you an oven near 900 °F (480 °C) and a pizza ready in 60 to 90 seconds, with a soft cornicione and leopard spotting. Allergens are handled on the menu and in the dining room.
48: The case prices to the market rather than to a wish: the Margherita at $18, other pizzas from $15-16 for a Marinara up to $20-24 for specialties, which is where the Neapolitan-style menus we reviewed sit. Recipes go by their own names: Margherita, Marinara, Diavola, Capricciosa. The menu rounds out with five starters and three desserts. The shop sells beer and wine only, with no full liquor. For off-premise there are two routes: pickup at the shop, with no commission, and third-party delivery marketplaces, which are capped. There is no in-house delivery.
49: The average check in the case is {{ticket}} per cover excluding sales tax, which is {{precio_menu}} with tax included. In the dining room it is made up of half a starter, a pizza, about 1.2 drinks and the occasional dessert or coffee. Food makes up {{comida_pct}} of sales and beverages {{bebida_pct}}, all of it beer, wine, soft drinks and coffee. Third-party marketplaces carry {{plataforma_pct}} of sales, and the rest is dine-in and direct pickup. At that check, cost of goods is {{cogs_pct}} of sales, which leaves a gross margin of {{margen_bruto_pct}}, and prime cost, which is cost of goods plus labor, is {{prime_cost_pct}}.
50: Neapolitan-style vs VPN-certified: what you can put on your menu. In the United States we found no federal rule that restricts the word Neapolitan on a menu, and the European protection of the name Pizza Napoletana has no effect here, so you can write Neapolitan-style on your sign. VPN is different: the Associazione Verace Pizza Napoletana (AVPN) is a private, voluntary seal. Certification costs $2,500, plus $300 for the inspection and $400 a year to renew in the USA and Canada, and it asks for an open location (no food trucks), a wood-fired dome oven at about 900 °F (480 °C), and dough and ingredients that follow its rules. Gas or electric ovens do not qualify. The risk is saying VPN-certified without the certificate, which is misleading advertising. That is why the case menu says Margherita, Marinara and Diavola, with long-fermented dough and a wood-fired oven, and the shop calls itself Neapolitan-style.
53: Demand for pizza in the United States is better read through what people search for than through market-size estimates of doubtful origin. According to DataForSEO, in October 2026 Google US shows 201,000 monthly searches for neapolitan pizza, 90,500 for new york style pizza, 49,500 for pizza shop, 18,100 for neapolitan style pizza and 8,100 for neapolitan pizza dough recipe. The trade searches a lot: pizza oven commercial gets 4,400 and wood fired pizza oven commercial 480. The person about to open searches far less: pizza shop business plan has about 320 a month (up about 6.5 times in six months), and how much does it cost to open a pizza shop or how to start a pizza business about 110 each. People who open a pizza shop decide with data, not with a single search.
54: The market itself is large and mostly independent. According to PMQ's Pizza Power Report 2026, the United States has about 75,000 pizzerias doing roughly $49.6 billion a year, and more than half are independents with fewer than 10 locations. The same report cites Datassential: of more than 1,000 openings, only 2 closed within 12 months, so the claim that 90% of pizzerias fail is a myth. For delivery, we found no reliable national share of sales, and Neapolitan-style dough travels worse than most dishes. That is why the plan caps marketplaces at {{plataforma_pct}} of sales. A neighborhood pizza shop lives mostly on its dining room, and delivery adds reach without becoming the business.
55: On prices, a review of menus in October 2026 shows the Margherita at $18 at Bufalina in Austin, TX, and $18.49 at via Marina in Des Moines, IA, with a high of $24 at Tutta Bella in the Seattle area, a large metro. Specialties run $20-24 and the Marinara $15-16. The median of the table-service menus we could confirm is $18-18.49, which is where the case puts its Margherita: a neighborhood price, not a destination-restaurant price. Check the menus in your area before you set yours: the median is a reference, not a rule, and your neighborhood may pay more or less.
56: With Month 1 in September, the plan spreads sales with seasonality. December, Month 4, is the peak thanks to office and group dinners; January and February, Months 5 and 6, are the softest; the patio lifts April through June; and August dips, because locals travel and nobody wants to sit near an oven at 900 °F (480 °C) in 100 °F weather. Between the best month and the worst, the spread is modest: a neighborhood pizza shop is a fairly flat business. Opening in September helps cash, because the ramp-up falls in medium and strong months, the holidays arrive with a crowd already in the habit, and January and February arrive with the reserve intact.
57: The gap is clear. What shows up on Google for how to open a pizza shop is generic guides, forum threads and templates with investment ranges and no breakdown. Few of them cover Neapolitan-style versus VPN-certified on the menu, the wood-fired oven question (a UL 2162-listed oven, the flue and the fire marshal), the beer and wine license, the sales tax on take-out, or the cash left after marketplace commissions. This plan does, with an Excel you can change.
58: Demand carries risks that the plan names. A price war from national delivery chains and grocery-store pizza puts pressure on the check. Marketplaces, with their commissions and promotions, eat your margin if you let them grow. The space is the filter: without approval for a flue to the roof there is no wood-fired oven, and you check it before you sign. And August, with the locals away, is a short-cash month. The plan covers this with a marketplace cap, a working capital reserve and scenarios in the Excel.
61: Before you set any price, draw the map of who competes with you in your neighborhood and your city. In pizza the competition comes from six sides: national delivery chains, Italian sit-down chains in shopping centers, craft Neapolitan-style pizzerias in the big cities, the classic neighborhood pizza shop, grocery-store pizza, and delivery-only kitchens.
62: Porter's five forces look like this in a pizza shop. Supplier power is moderate: flour, tomatoes and cheese can be bought in many places, but Italian imports and firewood depend on a few distributors and rise with the market. Buyer power is high, because guests switch shops or apps with one tap and compare prices. The threat of new entrants is medium: opening a pizza shop is easy, but with a wood-fired oven the barrier is the space with an approved flue and the investment. The threat of substitutes is high, because a guest can eat a burger, tacos or a grocery-store pizza. Rivalry is intense, with permanent deals from the chains. The defense is a different dough, an oven in plain view and a neighborhood that comes back.
63: The direct competitors are neighborhood pizza shops and craft Neapolitan-style places, which charge a high check and have waitlists. Behind them come the national delivery chains, with permanent promotions, and the Italian sit-down chains in shopping centers. On the substitute side are frozen and refrigerated grocery-store pizza and delivery-only kitchens. Your edge is the wood-fired oven in view, the dough of the day and a short menu with Italian ingredients. There is one more that counts: honesty in the name. A shop that claims VPN certification it does not hold risks having to pull the claim from its menu, its website and its marketplace listings.
64: The barriers to entry are compliance and cash. Opening means plan review, a health permit, a building permit, a certificate of occupancy and a business license, plus a beer and wine license from the state and the city that can take several months. The space is the filter: with a wood-fired oven, ask the fire marshal in writing whether you need a hood, whether you need fire suppression and what the UL 2162 file number is, because NFPA 96 and your local fire and mechanical code decide. Add the patio permit and the investment in oven, hood and build-out. Check everything with your city before you sign the lease.
65: Four factors decide whether it works. The first is the product: long-fermented dough, done well and the same every day, and a short menu that executes fast. The second is the site: a neighborhood street with foot traffic, a space that can take a flue and a patio that helps from April to October. The third is cost control: plate costing for every pizza, cost of goods and firewood, which burns by the hour of fire and not by the pizza and has a line of its own ({{lena_ano}} a year in the case). The fourth is the team: a steady pizzaiolo and a dining room that looks after guests, because a neighbor's recommendation sells more than any ad.
66: The SWOT of this concept is clear. Strengths: a wood-fired oven in view, dough made fresh daily, a short menu with Italian ingredients and a gross margin of {{margen_bruto_pct}} in year 1. Weaknesses: a high investment, a space with flue requirements and a thin net margin of {{margen_neto_a1}}. Opportunities: a trade that searches a lot, a loyal neighborhood and the office and group dinners of December. Threats: price wars, marketplace commissions and the risk of claiming a VPN certification you do not hold. The defense for each weak point lies in the product, the dining room and pickup at the shop.
69: The marketing strategy starts in the neighborhood and follows the calendar. In September you open with a tasting for the neighbors, nearby shops and schools. After that the oven in view, the pizza of the week and the patio, as soon as April arrives, carry the message. In December come office and group dinners, which book ahead and are best offered with a set menu. The menu carries the name of each recipe, clearly, and says Neapolitan-style without claiming a certification, in the dining room, on the website and on the marketplaces. It all points at one thing: getting the neighbor to come back.
70: Social media is the showcase for the oven. Post the oven build, the first fire, the dough as it ferments and the pizza of the week. Photos and short videos in natural light, with the flame and the pizzaiolo's hands stretching the dough, work better than a logo or long text. Reply to comments and messages, share what your guests post and show the daily work, including the dining room team. Three or four posts a week, kept up, are worth more than a burst followed by silence. And remember to link the menu and the hours in your profile.
71: Your Google Business Profile is your best free ad, because nearly everyone looking for a pizza shop nearby checks it. Complete it with photos of the oven, the dining room and the patio, and keep the lunch and dinner hours current, including the Monday closure and the two weeks in January. Claim your Yelp page too. Reply to every review, the bad ones as well, in a calm tone and with a solution. Ask for the review when the guest is happiest, at the table or when picking up the order, without pushing.
72: Local outreach starts at your door. Hold an opening tasting for the neighborhood and bring samples to the shops, offices and schools nearby. In December, offer office and group dinners with a set menu and an early booking. Loyalty can be simple: a stamp card or a pizza-of-the-month club is enough to bring guests back. No conversion figures are estimated here, because they depend on your neighborhood and how you work it: measure them yourself from the first month.
73: Marketplace or in-house delivery is a numbers decision. The plan sells {{plataforma_pct}} of its sales through third-party delivery marketplaces and pays a commission of {{comision_pct}} on those orders. Published tiers run from 15% to 30% on DoorDash and from 20% to 30% on Uber Eats, with Grubhub's marketing and delivery fees on top, plus promotions and the cardboard box. Your own driver costs wages, employer payroll taxes, hired and non-owned auto insurance and fuel, and in most states he or she must be a W-2 employee, so check your state. It tends to pay only with enough volume or a short, dense delivery zone, and it carries labor risk without the marketplace's storefront.
74: Pickup at the shop pays no marketplace commission, so push it with price. A small discount on an order picked up costs less than the marketplace commission and brings the guest to your door, where he or she can see the oven and order a dessert. There is a product reason too: soft Neapolitan-style dough travels worse than most dishes, and that is why the plan's ceiling is {{plataforma_pct}}. If the guest picks up, the pizza leaves the oven and arrives hot.
75: The marketing budget in the case is {{marketing_anual}} a year, mostly for photography, local ads and the tasting. The brand, website, photos and launch are separate, inside the startup costs ({{inv_lanzamiento}}). With that money, what pays best is cheap and steady: the Google profile, the photos of the oven and the relationship with the neighborhood.
